speaker: John Jumper
title: He won a Nobel here for AlphaFold. Then he left. - John Jumper
question: In deep learning, how much should architectures explicitly enforce intermediate concepts versus letting representations emerge from predictive training?
guest: This question of representations is very important, and far less important in the explicit way than people believed five years ago. Many things AlphaFold does, it does without being forced by its code, because it had to learn good intermediate representations to make a strong predictive model of the data. The most seductive idea in machine learning is thinking, "There's a concept I know must exist in the end, so I'll put a named module in my code or force disentangled representations with an intermediate loss." That's reasonable to test, but what we've actually seen is that many capabilities needed for intelligence develop by desperately trying to predict the next token really well. They don't develop merely because you predict next tokens; they develop because you do an extraordinarily good job at it. Those generalized representations are forced very slowly with data—things go up linearly with the exponent of effort, as we see in scaling laws—and what we still don't know is how to get them cheaper.

points.core: Explicitly hardcoding named concept modules into architectures usually underperforms emergent representations.
points.note: Accept: manually designing explicit concept bottlenecks or disentangled intermediate losses rarely matching representations learned end-to-end from the objective. Do not credit: generic praise for end-to-end learning without contrasting it against explicit concept-module design.

points.core: Useful internal concepts emerge only when models achieve extraordinarily accurate predictions.
points.note: Accept: representations not arising merely from using a next-token or predictive loss, but from pushing predictive accuracy to an extremely high level. Do not credit: claiming next-token prediction automatically yields intelligence at any accuracy level.

points.core: Acquiring emergent representations is expensive because quality scales only logarithmically with data.
points.note: Accept: log-linear scaling laws where representation quality grows linearly with the exponent of data or compute effort, making emergence slow and costly. Do not credit: vague statements that deep learning needs lots of data without mentioning slow/logarithmic scaling returns.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
As a default, enforce little and let representations emerge; add explicit structure only where you have a specific reason. That is a judgment call rather than a settled result, but the evidence leans one way.

The historical pattern (Sutton's "bitter lesson") is that general architectures trained on predictive objectives at scale tend to overtake systems with hand-designed intermediate concepts. Enforced concepts cap performance when the chosen concepts are incomplete or wrong. Concept bottleneck models illustrate this: they often trade accuracy for interpretability, and the bottleneck can leak non-concept information anyway, undermining the interpretability it was meant to buy.

Explicit structure earns its place in three cases. One is scarce data, where strong priors (convolution, equivariance, physical constraints) substitute for examples. Another is known symmetries or laws, as in molecular modelling. The last is when you need human intervention, auditing, or guarantees, such as in medical or safety-critical settings.

A useful middle path is soft enforcement: auxiliary losses, weak architectural biases, or post-hoc probing and interpretability tools on emergent representations, which keep capacity while recovering some transparency.

Enforced concepts cap performance when the chosen concepts are incomplete or wrong.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In general, architectures should let representations emerge freely from end-to-end predictive training whenever data and compute are abundant, reserving explicit concept enforcement for low-data, physically governed, or safety-critical settings. Echoing Rich Sutton’s "bitter lesson," general-purpose networks trained on broad predictive objectives consistently outperform architectures built around human-defined intermediate concepts, which rarely capture the subtle, distributed statistical structure that complex tasks require. Hard architectural constraints, such as strict concept bottleneck models, often sacrifice accuracy when predefined concepts are incomplete or suffer from "concept leakage," smuggling unintended shortcut signals through the bottleneck anyway.

Explicit intermediate structure remains worthwhile mainly when labeled data is scarce, exact physical symmetries or causal mechanisms are known, or high-stakes domains like medicine require humans to audit and intervene directly on intelligible variables. Even then, modern practice favors soft alignment over rigid bottlenecks: letting unconstrained backbones learn rich emergent features via predictive training, while using residual concept layers, auxiliary supervision, or sparse autoencoders to expose and steer interpretable concepts without throttling representational capacity.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly let representations emerge, and enforce concepts only where you have a specific reason to. The "bitter lesson" record backs this up: hand-designed intermediate stages like parse trees, phoneme pipelines and engineered vision features kept losing to end-to-end models trained on more data and compute. Imposed concepts tend to be a human guess at the right abstraction. They act as a bottleneck, and they break when the task or distribution changes.

Explicit structure still pays off in three cases. The first is a real inductive bias that matches the domain, such as convolution's translation equivariance, graph symmetries or physical conservation laws. These save data without limiting what the model can express. The second is when you need interpretability or the ability to intervene, as in medicine or safety. Concept-bottleneck models let you inspect and edit predictions, though they often lose some accuracy and can leak information around the bottleneck. The third is when data is scarce or supervision is weak, so a prior has to fill the gap.

A practical middle path is to train end-to-end, then use probing, sparse autoencoders or other interpretability tools to find concepts after the fact. Add soft auxiliary losses only where you can show they help generalization.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
In general, deep learning architectures should let representations emerge from predictive training by default, and enforce explicit intermediate concepts only when specific constraints demand it. Experience consistently shows that when data and compute are abundant, end-to-end predictive objectives discover richer, more transferable abstractions than human-designed bottlenecks, which often cap performance by discarding subtle, task-relevant signal.

Explicitly enforcing intermediate concepts—through concept bottleneck models, symbolic modules, or hard physical constraints—becomes worthwhile when data is scarce, out-of-distribution generalization depends on known invariants, or high-stakes applications require auditability, intervention, and formal guarantees. Even then, rigid supervision over intermediate states can be brittle if the chosen concepts are incomplete or misspecified.

The practical sweet spot is to rely on light, structural inductive biases rather than prescribed ontologies. Encode broad invariances or symmetries in the architecture, and use auxiliary losses or post-hoc interpretability tools to encourage and inspect structure without choking gradient flow. Only make intermediate concepts mandatory when transparency, controllability, or domain fidelity matters more than peak predictive accuracy.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Let most representations emerge from predictive training, and explicitly enforce intermediate concepts where they serve a concrete purpose. A concept bottleneck makes sense when people need to inspect or correct a model’s reasoning and the available concepts capture most of what the task requires. A hard bottleneck can hurt accuracy when concept labels are noisy or the concept set omits useful information.

If concepts are useful but incomplete, an auxiliary concept-prediction loss can encourage the model to learn them while leaving room for other features. If users need to intervene, test whether correcting a concept changes the prediction as intended. A model can predict concepts accurately while relying on a separate path for its decisions.

Choose the strength of the constraint by comparing predictive accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, and the effect of concept corrections. Use the weakest constraint that delivers the behavior you need.

points.why: The response favors letting representations emerge by default but only says hard bottlenecks can hurt when concept labels are noisy or incomplete, leaving the usual performance comparison unstated.
The response invokes predictive training without stating that useful internal concepts require extraordinarily accurate predictions to emerge.
The response gives no account of logarithmic returns to data or compute or how those returns make emergence costly.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Enforce intermediate concepts when you have a clear reason to rely on them. A known symmetry can justify a hard architectural constraint. If a clinician needs to correct a model’s assessment of a finding and see how that changes its diagnosis, routing the prediction through explicit findings can make that possible. But if those findings omit relevant evidence, the same constraint can hurt accuracy.

When concepts are informative but incomplete, a middle ground is to train the model to predict them alongside the main target while leaving room to learn other features. That can guide learning, though an accurate concept prediction alone doesn’t show that the model used the concept. If prediction is the sole goal and the proposed concepts are speculative, start with learned representations. Compare the alternatives on the outcomes that matter, including performance under likely distribution shifts and, where relevant, whether correcting a concept improves the final decision.
